title: Vocabulary: Words About Ceremonies
summary: Words used for traditional titles, festivals, rituals, naming, initiation and marriage, with an example sentence for each.

p: A strong vocabulary helps you in comprehension, summary and essay writing. This week's words come from culture, institutions and ceremonies. They appear often in WAEC and NECO passages about African life and history.
A ceremony is a formal act or series of acts performed in a set order, usually to mark an important occasion.
Installation is the formal ceremony of placing someone in a new position of authority. Example: The installation of the new Obi was attended by guests from across the country.
Investiture is the formal act of giving someone the authority and symbols (such as a staff or medal) of an office. Example: The investiture included the handing over of the sacred staff.
Homage is a public show of respect or loyalty to a superior, such as a king. Example: The chiefs came to pay homage to their new monarch.

Coronation is the ceremony of crowning a king or queen. A sceptre is a decorated staff that a ruler carries as a symbol of power. Regalia are the special clothes, jewellery and ornaments worn or carried by a ruler on state occasions: the crown, beaded necklaces and embroidered robes of an Oba are his regalia.
A festival is a day or period of celebration, usually for religious or cultural reasons. Example: The Eyo Festival in Lagos is a colourful display of culture and history.

A ritual is a solemn ceremony made up of actions done in a set order. Libation is the pouring of a drink, such as palm wine or gin, on the ground as an offering to a god, spirit or ancestor. A masquerade is a performer or group of performers in masks and costumes, often representing ancestral spirits. A carnival is a public festival with processions, music, dancing and masquerades. A procession is a number of people or vehicles moving forward in an orderly way as part of a ceremony.
Initiation is a rite of passage that marks entrance into a group or society, often with special rituals. Example: The young men went through a hard initiation into the age-grade society.
A rite of passage is a ceremony that marks an important stage in life, such as birth, puberty, marriage or death.

Dowry and bride price: in some places dowry means what the bride brings to her husband, while bride price (common in West Africa) is money or property that the groom's family gives to the bride's family.

activity: Write one meaningful sentence for each of these words: regalia, initiation, homage, masquerade, rite of passage. Then write a 100-word paragraph about a cultural festival in your area, using at least five of this week's words and underlining them.

title: Vocabulary: Words About Institutions
summary: Words for the rules, customs and structure of a society: norms, customs, tradition, taboo, social class, caste, kinship, family types, polygamy and monogamy.

p: An institution is an established organisation or foundation (such as a school), or the established laws, practices and customs of a society.
Norms are the unwritten rules that tell us what behaviour is acceptable in a group. Example: In many parts of Nigeria it is a social norm for children to kneel or bow when greeting elders.
A custom is a traditional and widely accepted way of behaving that belongs to a particular society, place or time. Example: The custom of celebrating the New Yam festival is centuries old.

Tradition is the passing of customs or beliefs from one generation to the next. Morality is the set of principles about right and wrong. A taboo is a custom that forbids or restricts a practice, person, place or thing. Example: In that community it is a taboo to whistle at night.

A custom is something people are expected to do, such as greeting elders in a special way. A taboo is something people are forbidden to do, such as speaking a sacred name. Both are part of a society's culture.

Social class is a division of society based on social and economic status. A caste is a rigid class system that a person is born into and cannot leave. Example: The caste system, though officially abolished, still influences social life in some societies.
Kinship is a blood relationship, or a sharing of common origins.
A nuclear family is a couple and their dependent children. An extended family includes grandparents, aunts, uncles, cousins and other relatives.
Polygamy is having more than one wife or husband at the same time. Monogamy is being married to one person at a time.

title: Vocabulary: African Arts and Culture
summary: Words for the arts of Africa: sculpture, griot, folklore, lyrics and age grades, with practice on using them in writing.

p: Sculpture is the art of making two- or three-dimensional forms by carving (wood, ivory) or casting (bronze). The Benin bronzes and Ife heads are famous African sculptures.
A griot is a West African historian, storyteller, praise singer, poet or musician who keeps oral tradition alive.
Folklore is the traditional beliefs, customs and stories of a community, passed on by word of mouth.
Lyrics are the words of a song.

An age group or age set is a social category of people of about the same age who share status, rights and duties and are initiated together. Example: The age group in charge of road maintenance this year is the Umu Chineke.

sections.h: Using new words in your own writing
p: To learn a word, use it. Write a sentence about something you really know. Weak: The griot is a griot. Better: At the wedding, the griot praised both families in song and recalled the deeds of their ancestors.
Remember to use the word in the correct form. For example, folklore is uncountable and takes a singular verb: Folklore is an important part of our culture.

sections.h: Revision list for the whole week
p: Ceremonies: installation, investiture, homage, coronation, sceptre, regalia, festival, ritual, libation, masquerade, carnival, procession, initiation, rite of passage, dowry. title: Spoken English: The Falling Tone
summary: What intonation is, what the nucleus is, and when to use the falling tone: statements, commands and Wh- questions.

p: Intonation is the rise and fall of the pitch (the high or low note) of your voice when you speak. It is the music of the language. It carries meaning beyond the words: it shows whether you are giving a fact, asking a question or showing surprise. Wrong intonation can cause confusion even if your grammar is perfect.
In every utterance one word is stressed more than the others. This is the nucleus (or tonic syllable). The movement of the voice, called the glide, happens on the nucleus.
Symbol: a downward arrow before the nucleus. The voice falls from a higher to a lower note. The falling tone gives a sense of finality, certainty and completeness. It sounds definite and confident.

Use the falling tone for: (a) ordinary statements: My name is \Bola. She lives in \London. It's a beautiful \day. (b) commands: Shut the \door. Go to your \room. \Stop. (c) information questions (Wh- questions, which need a specific answer): What is your \name? Where are you \going? How did you \do it?

Say the sentence aloud and listen for your voice dropping on the nucleus. Try a deep breath, say the word before the nucleus on a middle note, then let the nucleus start high and slide down. Practise with a friend and record yourself if possible.

title: Spoken English: The Rising Tone and the Fall-Rise
summary: When to use the rising tone: yes/no questions, lists, surprise and polite requests; and the fall-rise tone for doubt.

p: Symbol: an upward arrow before the nucleus. The pitch rises from a lower to a higher note. The rising tone gives a sense of incompleteness, uncertainty, politeness or a request for confirmation.

Use it for: (a) Yes/No questions: Is your name /Bola? Are you going /home? Did you see the /film? (b) Lists: the tone rises on each item and falls on the last, to show the list is finished: I bought some /apples, some /oranges and some \bananas. (c) Surprise or disbelief, to turn a statement into a question: You're leaving al/ready? He won the /lottery? (d) Polite requests: Can you help me, /please?
(Some printed notes write the nucleus of 'He won the lottery?' with a falling arrow. A question of surprise or disbelief uses the rising tone, so the correct mark is lott/ery.)

The fall-rise tone (the voice falls and then rises) is common in British English. It often shows hesitation, doubt or a slight correction. Example: It's good... (but it could be better). I like him... (but I don't trust him).

sections.h: Changing the meaning by moving the nucleus
p: The nucleus changes the meaning. Take I didn't say he stole the money. Stress I: someone else said it. Stress say: I only hinted it. Stress he: I said someone else stole it. Stress stole: he did something else with it. Stress money: he stole something else.

title: Nouns: Types of Nouns
summary: Proper, common, collective, abstract, concrete, countable and uncountable nouns, with a common error and its correction.

p: Proper nouns are the specific names of people, places and organisations; they begin with a capital letter: Chinua, Lagos, Nigeria, United Nations, Christmas. City is a common noun, but Port Harcourt is a proper noun.
Common nouns are general names for a person, place, thing or idea: woman, country, river, happiness, month.
Collective nouns name a group as one unit: a choir of singers, a board of directors, a pride of lions, a school of fish, a flock of birds, a fleet of ships, a bunch of bananas, a set of tools.
In British English a collective noun can take a singular verb (the group as a unit: The team is playing well) or a plural verb (the members as individuals: The team are putting on their boots).

Abstract nouns name ideas, qualities, states or feelings that you cannot see, touch, smell, taste or hear: bravery, freedom, knowledge, poverty, beauty, childhood. Concrete nouns name things you can perceive with the senses: rain, sand, whisper, perfume, sugar.

Countable nouns can be counted and have a singular and a plural: one book, three books; a chair, several chairs. Uncountable (mass) nouns cannot be counted. They have no plural form and take a singular verb: furniture, advice, information, water, equipment.

Common error: I have many furnitures. Correct: I have a lot of furniture, or I have many pieces of furniture. Likewise: He gave me good advice (not advices). Use a piece of, an item of or a bit of with uncountable nouns.

title: Nouns: Forming Plurals
summary: Regular plural rules and irregular, zero and foreign plurals that are often used in academic English.

p: Add -s to most nouns: dog, dogs; table, tables.
Add -es to nouns that end in -s, -ss, -x, -z, -sh, -ch: bus, buses; box, boxes; church, churches.
If a noun ends in a consonant plus -y, change -y to -ies: baby, babies; country, countries. (If a vowel comes before -y, just add -s: boy, boys.)
Some nouns that end in -o add -es: potato, potatoes; tomato, tomatoes; hero, heroes. Others add -s: photo, photos; piano, pianos. There is no perfect rule, so learn them.
Many nouns that end in -f or -fe change to -ves: leaf, leaves; wife, wives; knife, knives. Exceptions: chief, chiefs; roof, roofs; belief, beliefs.
Vowel change: man, men; woman, women; foot, feet; tooth, teeth; mouse, mice.
Zero plurals (no change): sheep, deer, series, species, aircraft.
-en plurals: child, children; ox, oxen.

These come from Latin and Greek and are used often in academic English: datum, data; criterion, criteria; phenomenon, phenomena; analysis, analyses; crisis, crises; index, indices (or indexes); syllabus, syllabi (or syllabuses).
Note: criteria and phenomena are already plural. Say one criterion, two criteria.

title: Noun Phrases
summary: What a noun phrase is, its parts (determiner, pre-modifiers, headword, post-modifiers) and its grammatical functions in a sentence.

p: A noun phrase (NP) is a word or group of words that does the work of a single noun in a sentence. It always has a main noun, the headword. Structure: (determiner) + (pre-modifiers) + HEADWORD + (post-modifiers).

Determiners: a, an, the, this, that, my, your, numbers. Pre-modifiers: adjectives or other nouns before the headword. Post-modifiers: groups of words after it, such as prepositional phrases (of the king) or relative clauses (who lives next door).
Examples, getting longer: the car; the sleek, black car; the sleek, black car parked in the driveway; the sleek, black car which he bought last week. In all of them the headword is car.

A noun phrase can be: (a) Subject: [The diligent student] passed the exam. (b) Object of the verb: She admired [the diligent student]. (c) Complement: He became [a diligent student]. (d) Object of a preposition: She gave the award to [the diligent student].

In the sentence The three talented musicians from the village played a beautiful melody, the subject is the noun phrase the three talented musicians from the village. Its headword is musicians. The object is a beautiful melody, with headword melody.

title: Expository Essay: Features
summary: The purpose of an expository essay and its five hallmarks: clarity, objectivity, formal tone, logical organisation and evidence.

p: Continuous writing (essay writing) carries a large share of the marks in your English examination. An expository essay does not tell a story, paint a picture or win a debate. It explains, clarifies and informs. Think of yourself as a knowledgeable teacher or a careful reporter, presenting facts and examples in an organised way.
1. Clarity and conciseness: it is easily understood; use simple words where they will do.

2. Objectivity and impersonality: it is based on facts, not feelings. Avoid I believe, I think, in my opinion. Weak: I feel that corruption is bad for the country. Strong: Corruption has clearly harmful effects on national development.
3. Formal and academic tone: no contractions (write do not, not don't), no slang.
4. Logical organisation: a clear five-paragraph structure (the next unit).
5. Evidence-based support: every claim is supported with facts, examples, statistics or reasons.

Narrative essays tell a story. Descriptive essays paint a picture. Argumentative essays take a side and try to persuade. Expository essays explain. Read the topic: words like Explain, Discuss the causes of, Write on the importance of usually signal an expository essay.

title: Expository Essay: Structure
summary: The introduction (hook, background, thesis statement), body paragraphs (topic sentence, supporting details, link) and conclusion (restated thesis, summary, final thought).

p: The introduction is the foundation, the body paragraphs are the walls and the conclusion is the roof.

It has three parts. The hook is a general statement to catch the reader's interest: a striking fact, a rhetorical question or a short quotation. The background narrows down from the hook and gives context or a definition. The thesis statement is the most important sentence of the essay. It states clearly the main purpose and the points that the body will explain.
Example thesis: The scourge of drug abuse, driven mainly by peer pressure and economic hardship, damages the health and social standing of the individual and weakens the wider community.

Each paragraph develops one main idea that supports the thesis. It begins with a topic sentence (the main idea, linked to the thesis). Then come the supporting details: facts, examples and explanations that answer How? Why? Can I give an example? The paragraph ends with a concluding or linking sentence. Use transition words: furthermore, in addition, consequently, as a result, on the other hand.
It restates the thesis in different words (do not copy it), summarises the main points and ends with a final thought: a remark, warning, prediction or recommendation.

title: Planning an Expository Essay: Drug Abuse
summary: A complete model plan: brainstorming ideas, writing an outline and building the thesis, topic sentences and conclusion for an essay on drug abuse.

p: Write down all your ideas before you write the essay. For drug abuse: What is it? The harmful or addictive use of narcotic substances. Causes: peer pressure, unemployment, poverty, curiosity, mental health problems, poor parental guidance. Effects on the individual: addiction, mental illness, organ damage, dropping out of school, financial ruin, crime. Effects on society: more crime, broken families, a burden on hospitals, loss of workers. Solutions: public education, stricter law enforcement, job creation, rehabilitation centres.
Title: The Menace of Drug Abuse in Contemporary Society.

Introduction: hook (a statistic or a rhetorical question about young people and drugs); background (define drug abuse and say how common it is); thesis: Drug abuse, a complex problem fuelled by social and economic factors, leads to devastating health consequences for the individual and threatens the safety and unity of society.

Body 1, causes. Topic sentence: The descent into drug abuse is often triggered by peer influence and economic hardship. Details: how peer pressure works; how unemployment leads to idleness and despair.

Body 2, effects on the individual. Topic sentence: The consequences for the user are severe, affecting both physical health and social standing. Details: addiction as a disease of the brain; lung damage and overdose; stigma and isolation.

Body 3, effects on society. Topic sentence: The effects of drug abuse extend far beyond the individual, destabilising families and communities. Details: theft and robbery to fund the habit; the emotional cost to families; the cost of policing and health care.

Conclusion: restate the thesis (In summary, the cycle of drug abuse, started by social and economic pressure, causes personal tragedy and wide social harm); summarise; final thought (A combined approach of education, economic empowerment and accessible rehabilitation is not just advisable but necessary).

Many examinations give a word limit, for example 400 words. Plan about 60 to 80 words for the introduction, 80 to 90 for each of three body paragraphs and 50 to 60 for the conclusion. Keep a margin so you do not exceed the limit.

title: Comprehension: Silent Reading Strategies
summary: Skimming, scanning and intensive reading, and when to use each one in the examination.

p: Comprehension is understanding, interpreting and judging what you read. In your SSCE examination it is a silent, timed skill. Silent reading is faster, helps you concentrate and lets you think about ideas without the distraction of reading aloud.

Purpose: to get the main idea or gist quickly. How: read the title and any headings; read the first and last paragraphs (they often contain the thesis and conclusion); read the first sentence of each paragraph; let your eyes move quickly and notice words in bold or italic or words that are repeated. Use it before reading a passage in detail.

Purpose: to find one piece of information quickly, such as a name, date or number. How: know exactly what you are looking for; move your eyes quickly over the text without reading every word; use cues such as numbers, capital letters or key words. Use it to answer a factual question.

Purpose: to understand all the details, arguments and implications. How: after skimming, read slowly, paragraph by paragraph; underline key points and unknown words; stop at the end of each paragraph and say its main point to yourself; ask: What is the author's main argument? What evidence is used? What is the tone? Use it when you must answer detailed questions.

sections.h: A good order in the examination
p: First skim the passage. Then read the questions. Then read intensively, scanning for facts. Answer in complete sentences in your own words unless you are asked to quote. Keep to the time.

title: Comprehension: Words in Context and Question Types
summary: Using synonym, antonym and example clues to find the meaning of words, and recognising the five kinds of comprehension questions.

p: An examination often asks the meaning of a word as used in the passage. The dictionary meaning may not fit, so use clues.

Synonym or restatement clue: the writer gives a meaning nearby. His obdurate nature, his stubborn refusal to change his mind, made negotiation impossible. (stubborn refusal to change his mind explains obdurate.)
Antonym or contrast clue: the writer gives an opposite. While the manager was often loquacious, his assistant was a man of very few words. (the contrast shows loquacious means talkative.)

Example clue: examples explain the word. The museum had various relics from the war, including torn uniforms, rusted weapons and old letters. (the examples show a relic is an old object from the past.)
1. Factual (direct): the answer is stated in the text. Key words: What is, Who, When, List. Scan for the information.
2. Inferential: the answer is implied, not stated. Key words: suggest, infer, imply, what conclusion can you draw. Combine the text with logical thinking.
3. Vocabulary in context: As used in the passage, what does X mean? Use the clues above.
4. Main idea or global: the central theme or purpose. Look at the title, the thesis in the first paragraph and the conclusion.

5. Reference or grammar: What does the word it refer to? What is the grammatical name and function of the expression? Look back to the nearest noun for a pronoun; name the construction (noun phrase, adverbial clause) and its job.

title: Comprehension Practice: Youth Restiveness
summary: A practice passage on youth restiveness with five questions of different types and model answers.

p: Read the passage silently first, then answer the questions.

Youth restiveness, a term that describes the agitated and often disruptive behaviour of a nation's young people, has become a gargantuan challenge in many developing countries. This phenomenon does not emerge from a vacuum. Its primary catalyst is the pervasive and debilitating spectre of unemployment. When a significant portion of the educated and able-bodied youth is left idle, their energies, which ought to be channelled towards productive ventures, are often diverted into social vices. Furthermore, the decay in societal values, where wealth is celebrated without questioning its source, makes the problem worse. Young people observe individuals with ostentatious lifestyles, often products of corruption, and are pressured to attain such wealth by any means necessary. This creates a fertile ground for political thuggery, cybercrime and armed robbery.

To curb this menace, a multi-pronged approach is essential. It is not enough to simply police the youth; we must create real economic opportunities. Revitalising the nation's industries, fostering entrepreneurship and a systematic re-orientation of values are the only long-term solutions to this endemic problem.
1. (Factual) What is the primary catalyst for youth restiveness? Answer: The primary catalyst is unemployment.
2. (Factual) Name two social vices. Answer: Political thuggery, cybercrime and armed robbery are mentioned. Any two are correct.
3. (Vocabulary) The meaning of ostentatious. Answer: Showy, meant to impress others, especially with wealth.

4. (Inferential) What does 'This phenomenon does not emerge from a vacuum' mean? Answer: Youth restiveness does not appear for no reason; it has definite causes, such as unemployment and the decay of values.
5. (Main idea) The author's purpose. Answer: To explain the causes of youth restiveness and to suggest ways of solving the problem.

(a) Three solutions in the last paragraph: reviving the nation's industries, encouraging entrepreneurship and a systematic re-orientation of values. (b) A multi-pronged approach means using several different methods at the same time. (c) The expression 'a pervasive and debilitating spectre of unemployment' is a noun phrase; here it is the complement of the verb (is) in 'Its primary catalyst is ...'. (d) Synonyms: gargantuan, huge; idle, unoccupied or jobless; endemic, widespread or constantly present.

Answer in complete sentences. Use your own words, but keep the meaning exactly. Do not copy long parts of the passage. Match your answer to the question word: list means give items, explain means give reasons.
